speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be very brief. My request to move adjournment of the House under Standing Order 52 relates to yesterday's decision regarding the softwood lumber tariff issue.
While we take comfort in part of the ruling from yesterday there is a particular part of the ruling that may prove to be very difficult for the province of British Columbia. In particular, the ruling has determined that the export of raw logs constitutes a subsidy.
I believe that goes to the heart of a government's ability to make decisions on how it manufactures or processes raw resources, in particular raw logs.
I think it has important and potentially serious implications for our ability to manage our resources. I would ask for your guidance and support on this, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I agree with the hon. member that there are certainly implications, probably good and bad, in the decision that was rendered yesterday, but at this point the conditions required to adjourn the House according to Standing Order 52 are not present.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Blais that Bill C-123, an act respecting the management of certain property seized or restrained in connection with certain offences, the disposition of certain property on the forfeiture thereof and the sharing of the proceeds of disposition therefrom in certain circumstances, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am in receipt of a notice of Mr. Nelson A. Riis (Kamloops): Madam Speaker, I motion under Standing Order 52(1) from the hon. appreciate this opportunity to return to debate on Bill member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley.	C-123.

May 7, 1993
Government Orders
When we left off before Question Period I was saying that there were a number of concerns. They will be raised at the committee stage but I want to put them clearly on the record.
One is the fact that this procedure of sharing the proceeds of crime between those participating in the successful conclusion of an inquiry or prosecution has been implemented in the United States where there is evidence that in some cases police departments have grown to view the prosecution of cases from which they are more likely to receive rewards in the form of the forfeiture of significant proceeds as being the most important cases to work on and proceed with.
Those crimes that do not involve the possibility of such a reward, such as crimes involving family violence, are not given the same attention that might have been given where there is not a dollar value attached.
I do not want to suggest for a moment that this would influence police departments in our country but it must be recognized that there is some possibility of this.
However this concern has also been alluded to by Department of Justice officials. It will be interesting for us to hear from the various witnesses in committee. I think it is fair to say that anything that would inadvertently shift the system away from responding to the needs of a community based on the degree of urgency or harm done and the potential for harm toward a greater interest in the number of dollars involved must be avoided.
I believe that the Solicitor General earlier today put this concern at rest, at least here on the floor of the House, when he said that it may not go directly to the police departments or to the agencies or departments involved but to those agencies that fund them. In other words, it is a bit of an arm's length relationship here.
The second concern we have is that there have been concerns expressed that the implementation of this program may be the thin edge of the wedge leading to police departments becoming more and more reliant upon proceeds of crime forfeitures for their base budget funding.
There is nothing in this bill to give any indication as to how this might be prevented. I am again just identifying concerns we will be raising in committee so that those who will be responding can be forewarned. In fact, details of how the funds are to be shared by the various levels of government are still under review although we have heard comments from the Solicitor General.
Another area of concern would be who will pay for the new office that would be struck. Obviously the new office will be established within the Department of Supply and Services. I think it is a fair question to ask. Whenever a new office, department or agency is being set up by government we ask where the money for that will come from. That is what the taxpayers of Canada are asking us to do at all times. In committee we will be asking: Who will fund this? Will it simply come from the estimates of the department? Will the proceeds of forfeited moneys from crimes be used to fund this office? Will it be shared between the various jurisdictions, for example federal, provincial, municipal and regional? These are questions that are fair to ask.
The last point is certainly frustrating in the sense that one of our primary concerns is that a significant share of the money forfeited as proceeds of crime go toward crime prevention and substance abuse prevention. This was one of the primary recommendations of the unanimous report on crime prevention tabled in this House by the chair of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General in February. It is certainly a recommendation that we in the New Democratic Party will support.
I noted with interest yesterday that when the member for Kitchener rose and introduced the government's psychoactive substances legislation he pointed out that for every dollar spent on prevention, and specifically the prevention of substance abuse, the government could expect to save $7 down the road in treatment and justice system costs. There is all kinds of evidence that $1 set aside for prevention would result time and time again in that $1 being saved a little bit further along the way.
I would like to simply say that we want to see this preventative initiative focused not only on hard drugs but on smoking and alcohol abuse as well.
May 7, 1993

We will have more to say in committee and I will leave my remarks at that.

Madam Speaker, I too am pleased to stand here and speak in this House on Bill C-123, which establishes a federal program to share forfeited proceeds of crime with other jurisdictions involved in federal drug and other federal criminal prosecutions.
I know the details of how the funds will be shared are still under review. Today individual police forces do not receive the money, but under the proposed legislation they would still not receive the money but the money would certainly go to the department that funds those same police forces, which is either the provincial or municipal government. In my case it would be the city of Nepean.
It also proposes to establish an office within the Department of Supply and Services to manage the restrained assets that have been seized in the particular federal crime cases. This office would also have an advisory function for law enforcement agencies.
Canada has had proceeds of crime legislation since 1989 but all the moneys and assets collected reverted to the federal government. In many cases this was seen as unfair to the provincial and municipal governments that assisted in cracking these cases. Many of these cases were under investigation for long periods of time and were very costly to local and provincial police departments. Problems have arisen with respect to the cost of managing seized or restrained assets.
In consultation with my own Nepean police services department I have been advised by the deputy chief of Nepean, Devon Fermoyle, that the Ontario police chiefs have called for a cost sharing of crime proceeds. The Ontario chiefs feel the money should be divided among the various levels involved in the cases because many of the raids-in fact probably all of the raids-do involve local forces in addition to the RCMP forces or the FBI. The moneys that are generated should also go to the municipal forces through the municipality.
Deputy Chief Fermoyle gave me one example of how in a recent bust in collaboration with a number of other levels they recovered $14,000 and yet the cost to the city of Nepean police department was $60,000. They really believe they should have been able to at least recover
Government Orders
their costs and they have not been able to do so until this point in time. Even if there is real property on sale the money goes to the federal agency and not to the municipal agencies.
In the United States there is quite a different situation. Say for example if the FBI, the RCMP and the tobacco-firearms department in the U.S.A. are involved. They had a big bust recently in the U.S. As a result the United States government handed over $100,000 to the Canadian government. Its system is very different from ours and the federal agency is able to put this money in its pocket and obviously the local forces should be able to receive some of this money.
We on this side of the house proposed a similar scheme to this in a recent policy paper on justice issues. We have been calling for legislation such as this for a good number of years now. We have recommended that the proceeds of any crime operation be split among all parties involved in the case and the percentages would depend upon each party's level of involvement.
Since 1989 I am told that only $60 million in assets has been seized through the current proceeds of crime legislation. Obviously someone is not doing one's job. A lot more money than that should have come into the coffers if somebody had been monitoring it and ensuring that the law enforcement agencies and the government were working very closely together to make sure that this money came in.
We on this side of the House want assurances from the Minister of Justice that the proceeds of crime will indeed find their way back to local and provincial police departments through their municipalities. We want to be certain that provincial and municipal governments will not just keep this money to build new roads or pay down their deficits.
As a 10-year member of a municipal council I know that they tend to shift money from one little pocket to another or from one little pay account to another or reserve account to another. I would certainly want to make sure that the municipalities direct this money right back into police service.
Not in Nepean.

"Not in Nepean", my colleague from Vanier says. This does happen in any municipality. I believe that the police forces are having a very difficult time these days. They have been cut back drastically due

May 7, 1993
Government Orders
to fiscal restraint and they need these additional funds as much as anybody else.
With regard to the proposed new office for the Department of Supply and Services, I think that is another area that we must monitor. Every time a new department is created we create a bureaucratic nightmare. I think we need to make sure that this office is efficiently run and efficiently established and that there is more clarification from the government on the exact function and role of this particular office.
Assurances also need to be given by the Minister of Justice that the proceeds of crime will definitely find their way back into the proper pockets as I mentioned a few minutes ago. Although the proposed new office is probably considered of a secondary nature with regard to this bill, I think we need to ensure that we have everything tied down if we are going to establish a new department.
I have a letter from the Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse. It concerns the proposed changes to the proceeds of crime legislation.
The Canadian Centre on Substance Abuse outlined a position paper that pertained to this matter that has been put out by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police. They met and jointly agreed on the importance of this legislation.
I do have a copy of that brief here and I would like to table it for the information of the Minister of Justice. It is important that when there are agencies such as these three I have mentioned that are standing in strong support of this legislation then it needs to be passed and our police services departments need to be the recipients of these funds. We must make sure that this legislation does goes through.
I wish I had had the opportunity to read this brief but it was just handed to me this moment. I have not had the time to read it but I think it is important that it is filed and that everyone is aware of it.
Again thank you for the opportunity of speaking in the House on this very important bill. I am sure that it will pass quickly.

Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to mention another point which so far has not been brought to the attention of the Solicitor General. It concerns a ski resort in Quebec.
Bill C-123 would authorize the minister to manage and dispose of property referred to in paragraph (b), and property that is from the proceeds of crime or offence-related property, when such property is forfeited to Her Majesty. It would provide that on taking possession or control thereof, the minister shall be responsible for the custody and management of the property.
When I started to look into the case of the ski resort in Quebec, I realized that it took a long time for the case to get started because there were so many searches and investigations. I believe it took about two years. At one point the forfeited property was operated, if I am not mistaken, by the RCMP. To have the RCMP operating a ski resort is positively mind boggling.
When we consider the amounts of money involved in these cases, as was said earlier by my colleagues, since 1989 all we have is $60 million, but $60 million is still $60 million. If my information is correct, the money is never deposited in a bank account and that has been the case for many years. We are talking about several million dollars that were deposited in a bank vault-this is cash-and will stay there until there is enough evidence, a sufficient number of searches have taken place and enough statements have been gathered to bring the case before the courts. Sometimes it can take years.
I think all this is incredible and pretty ridiculous. The time involved may be considerable because the procedure includes preliminary investigations, statements and searches, as I said before. The latter are initiated to find other properties, such as houses or cars, which the accused may own.
I think this is all quite unacceptable, and I will explain why. If for some reason the Crown does not gather enough evidence to lay charges it is obliged to return the money in whole or in part. Usually, as I said before, the money is put in a vault. However, when a decision is reached by the courts, it always allows for the accumulated interest. The courts always consider the real value of the money, not the amounts seized at the beginning of the investigation. This means the taxpayer has to pay the
May 7, 1993

interest on those amounts. I wonder why this money cannot be deposited in a trust account pending court proceedings. In this way Canadian taxpayers would not be stuck with paying millions of dollars in interest costs.
The brief that we have from the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police about the proceeds of crime recommends that the federal government proceed with the proposed ethics management office establishing an audit mechanism that includes other orders of government, that participating governments be involved in the development of fair procedures for the sharing of net forfeited assets, that the federal government in consultation with the orders of government develop a mechanism which would enable direct sharing of net proceeds with entitled parties and that guidelines be provided for the use of forfeited drug proceeds in accordance with the policy thrust of Canada's drug strategy.
As my other colleagues mentioned, we proposed a similar scheme to this one but I am not sure that anyone took a real hard look at the money that is stuck in a vault.
I am not talking about the money that has fingerprints on it or that was marked money in order to catch some of our drug traffickers. We are not even touching the bottom of the barrel. We are just skimming off the surface with our $60 million. Consequently once this money has filtered back down to the forces and to the levels of government that are paying the bill we could have many more millions.

We have to come up with a way to keep the money in an interest-bearing account. I have nothing against the office proposed by the minister, but that office should have a special, entirely separate bank account for the proceeds of money laundering.

We want the minister to assure us that the proceeds of these crimes will find their way back to local and provincial police departments. We do not want the bureaucracy eating all the money that is being made from the proceeds of crime.
This war against drugs is a difficult one. It may never be won. If we do not start putting the money back into fighting the drug lords then we will never win it.
Government Orders
I would like to see the minister amend this bill so that a trust account could be opened. It would be one that will not be bogged down by bureaucracy and the money will be available when the judges say it is available. It will earn interest in the meantime because we as taxpayers cannot afford any more expenses especially not from the laundering of drug money.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the need for the reform of sentencing in Canada has long been recognized by judges, parliamentarians, law reformers and members of the legal profession.
During the past 20 years there have been calls for reform from various committees, a royal commission and from the Law Reform Commission of Canada. More recently, the Canadian Sentencing Commission which reported in 1987 and in 1988, a report of the House committee, the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, made extensive recommendations regarding the reform of sentencing, conditional release and corrections.
Bill C-90 gives Canadians for the first time a say on the purpose and principles of criminal sentencing. Extensive consultations were carried out involving both justice professionals and representatives of the community.
These consultations followed joint publication by the Solicitor General and the Minister of Justice of directions for reform, sentencing, corrections and conditional release in July 1990. The changes proposed in this bill have been broadly accepted by criminal justice professionals, provinces and territories.
Together with Bill C-36 passed by Parliament last year, Bill C-90 presents a strong and unified approach to criminal justice. I believe that sentencing practices in Canada must consistently reflect values that Canadians have told us are important to them in the treatment of offenders. Considering the fact that criminal sanctions provide for one of the most serious intrusions of the state into the lives of individuals, the absence of a policy statement from the Parliament of Canada seems quite remarkable.
Bill C-90 provides courts with clear policy direction from Parliament. The bill states that the fundamental purpose of sentencing is to contribute to the maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society by imposing just sanctions. A statement of principles is set out, designed to establish a coherent framework of policy and process in sentencing matters and to bring consistency, fairness and accountability to the sentencing process. The establishment of a statement of the purpose and principles of sentencing has been endorsed by the Canadian Sentencing Commission, the standing committee and the former Law Reform Commission of Canada.
This is a large and detailed bill. I cannot discuss all of the provisions but would like to highlight a number which I feel are particularly important. I will start by elaborating on the statement of the purpose and principles of sentencing.
In addition to the fundamental purpose of sentencing, the bill sets out objectives which judges should consider when sentencing.
The objectives available to judges in this bill include denunciation, deterrence and separation of the offender from society. These are clearly appropriate sentencing objectives to apply to the 8 to 10 per cent of violent crime which is handled in our courts. This does not suggest, of course, that we can ever eliminate violence totally in our society. In absolute terms, wanton violence by deranged individuals is probably unavoidable except at a cost in terms of rights and freedoms which Canadians would be unwilling to accept.
May 7, 1993

The government is committed to strengthening the Canadian system of justice to ensure that it is inclusive and can respond to the needs and aspirations of all Canadians. It wants to ensure that Canada is a just and law abiding society with an accessible, efficient and fair system of justice. It wants to improve the protection of society so that Canadians are confident of their personal and community safety. It wants to build upon values and trends in the Constitution and the charter and to promote respect for rights and freedoms. This requires much more than simply more criminal sentencing. Bill C-90 provides other sentencing objectives which may be more appropriate for the majority of offenders.
The bill describes, for example, the objective of providing reparations for the harm done to both individuals and to the community. Also included is provision for promoting a sense of responsibility on the part of offenders and an acknowledgement of the harm done to victims and to the community. While having general application and importance to the community at large, these two objectives may be particularly appropriate to aboriginal communities which are interested in bringing the concept of healing to criminal justice.
The bill recognizes the objective of using the criminal justice system to assist in rehabilitating offenders. The concept of rehabilitation is at the core of much of what is done in our correctional systems at both the federal and provincial levels. It is the operational means of best ensuring the long-term protection of society. A rehabilitated offender contributes more to the protection of society than a warehoused criminal who will ultimately be released into society.
The bill also sets out principles through which the court may exercise its discretion. The fundamental principle is that a sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender. The court may take into consideration aggravating or mitigating circumstances. Sentences should be comparable for offenders who have committed similar acts in similar circumstances. Sentences should not be unduly long or harsh. In keeping with the fact that the majority of offenders are not violent and that preferable treatment is usually available in the community, this bill states that an offender should not be deprived of liberty if less restrictive alternatives may be
Government Orders
appropriate. The statement of purpose and principles of sentencing states that all available alternatives to imprisonment that are reasonable in the circumstances should be considered. This is so generally, but particularly in the case of aboriginal offenders.
The statement of the purpose and principles of sentencing, the changes to the Code respecting procedure and evidence, the restructuring of that part of the Code which deals with sentencing and the involvement of Parliament in sentencing policy will all serve to deal with identified sentencing problems such as unwanted disparity.
There is a provision in this bill requiring the reasons for sentence to be given in all cases. This measure will encourage well-reasoned decisions, assist courts of appeal and serve an educative function. Giving reasons will assist in making more clear what is intended by the courts and should enable the public to relate what is done in sentencing to the policy approved by Parliament. These changes should help to deal with the confused view of sentencing held by the public as described in the report of the standing committee and by the Canadian Sentencing Commission. This change will help us to evolve sound government policy in criminal justice with broad, better informed public support.
These proposals are designed to increase public accessibility to the law concerning sentencing and to make it more understandable and predictable. The bill includes a complete restructuring of Part XXIII of the Criminal Code of Canada. The current structure of the Criminal Code exhibits little legislative consideration of this important process. It provides little guidance to the courts or to the public respecting the policy which we intend. This restructuring brings together most of the provisions relating to sentencing within the Criminal Code and structures them to make them more logical and accessible. Structuring of Part XXIII in this way makes it more understandable and accessible to both criminal justice professionals and to the public. This should also help in dealing with the broad public misunderstanding of criminal justice.
Bill C-90 establishes rules of procedures and evidence which will bring greater consistency, fairness and accountability to the sentencing process. They will deal

May 7, 1993
Government Orders
with, for example, what information should be available to the court, powers that the court should have to obtain that information and how the information is considered. The judge must consider victim impact statements prepared according to the Criminal Code. The offender will have the right to speak to the sentence.
An innovative provision in this bill will bring into the Criminal Code a provision for alternative measures for adults. Alternative measures have two main aims: to prevent the continuation of criminal behaviour and to lessen the stigma of proceedings. They also promote community involvement and awareness by involving the community in measures themselves and by putting a greater emphasis on victim-offender reconciliation. Alternative measures programs can be used instead of formal court proceedings and have been found particularly appropriate for first time and non-violent offenders. Diverting less serious offenders away from courts means that scarce time and resources can be focused on more serious crime. In this way the bill gives further expression to the involvement of the community in dealing with criminal justice issues.
Bill C-90 reflects the conceptual framework within which the government sees the justice system being reorganized and made more broadly comprehensible. The underlying principle is that the Canadian justice system must serve all Canadians.
Second, our justice system must be responsive and fair to all Canadians. In my view this can best be achieved by inspiring confidence in a broadly cast system of justice. The system must be sensitive to the needs of all Canadians, take account of their distinctiveness and reflect basic Canadian values.
Third, our justice system must protect society. This means promoting means by which Canadians have confidence in their personal and community security. We are building on both individual rights and responsibilities.
This bill contributes to the maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society. Its adoption will be an historic step in the reform of law and practice of sentencing in Canada of which this Parliament can be so proud.
I move that Bill C-90 be read a second time.

Madam Speaker, it is awfully difficult, and with due respect to the member for South Shore for whom I have a good deal of respect, to listen to the words of the government relating to Bill C-90, about what a wonderful legislation it is and how it is going to be so helpful with all the things that it is going to do.
If the government really believes anything that it has put in that speech, then surely this bill would have been before the House before now. Frankly, it is an insult to the House that a bill that receives first reading on June 23, 1992 has to wait until May 1993 to be introduced for second reading.
How can the government possibly hope to convince anyone to believe that it supports this bill, its own legislation, when it waits practically 11 months to bring the legislation forward before a House of Commons that is going to be adjourned and go into a federal election probably within a matter of weeks? It is misleading and hypocritical of the government to deal with this legislation in the way it has so chosen.
What the government is doing is nothing more than show casing justice legislation. I think the interest of Canadians is not being well-served by this government's procedure of playing with legislation, playing with the cost of the House of Commons and using it for trivial little interludes of conversation which it wants to have passed on to the Canadian people as conscientious attempts to pass legislation.
It is offensive and it is truly repugnant. I frankly feel that it is a sham.
Certainly there are a lot of things in this legislation that would have been very helpful to have. If we sit well into the summer we can perhaps pass this bill.
This is not an incidental piece of legislation. This is not a minor bill. This is a very important bill. The parliamentary secretary mentioned Bill C-36. Bill C-36 should have waited until Bill C-90 was passed. Bill C-90 should have come before Bill C-36.
The fact is that the cart was before the horse. That is one thing. Then to wait for 11 months to bring the horse to the cart is irresponsible. I would hope that this bill will at least go to committee and that the government will follow it through that far and we will have at least some
May 7, 1993

dialogue in committee. If the government does not want to have it passed, let us at least have some pertinent conversation and some pertinent discussion on this very important issue.
The bill as the parliamentary secretary has said repeals all of the present Part XXIII of the Criminal Code, replacing it with an amended and reorganized version. It introduces in this legislation the concept of alternative measures for adults.
This program would be almost identical with that contained in the Young Offenders Act. This is a major step forward and I hope to state why I feel this way. Once again, I have a difficult time believing that the government really thinks this is a major step forward. If it did think this, the legislation would have come before the House well before now for second reading.
The alternative measures would include such things as community service and educational programs for those who have committed offences and whom the correctional and the justice systems feel can be rehabilitated. Accused persons however would have to accept responsibility for their crime and they would have to agree to participate in such a program.
If there is to be an alternative measure, we just cannot have the alternative measure put into effect for somebody who is accused unless that person will at least admit that he or she has committed a crime and is prepared to accept the alternative measure.
It is significant to mention too that not only have we wasted 11 months on this bill which could have been passed, but there is a long road ahead in dealing with the provinces. The provincial attorneys general would have to be responsible for establishing these alternative measures programs. We have known from the difficulties of implementing the Young Offenders Act. Rehabilitation and counselling for young offenders since 1978 is instigated by the provinces, as are training courses for a firearms acquisition certificate for those who use firearms.
Since 1978 we have been trying to get the provinces to work out a program. I do not know how hard this government has been trying but that is how long it has been. We still do not have these training programs in effect.
Government Orders
To try to work with the provincial attorneys general in setting up these alternative measures is not going to be an easy thing. This government has not done anything to try to bring forward alternative measures. How can we expect that when it has not even taken any time to bring forward its own enabling legislation that is supposed to do this. It introduced it in June 1992 and did not bring it forward for second reading until May 1993.
What we want to do as an opposition is at least, certainly on behalf of the Liberal Party, to indicate our good faith for this legislation. Unfortunately we do not have control over setting the agenda in the House of Commons. That is the government's responsibility. That is what the government House leader is supposed to do. However we will proceed and work on this given the opportunity. Unfortunately this is the first opportunity in 11 months we have had to deal with this bill and try to at least do something to bring it to reality.
The bill also sets out the fundamental purpose of sentencing to contribute to the maintenance of a just, peaceful and safe society. That is the fundamental purpose of sentencing: imposing just sanctions with certain listed objectives. These might include: denunciation of unlawful conduct, general and specific deterrence, separation of offenders from society, reparation of victims or the community, promotion of a sense of responsibility, acknowledgement of the harm done and, last, rehabilitation of offenders. These are considerations which we must have if we are going to have a meaningful correctional system and positive term of incarceration, if we can use the term positive.
We have to realize in this country that as much as we want correction and as much as we want deterrence the people we put into our correctional system are some day going to come out of our correctional system. We have to know whether these people are going to be able to have a chance to live law abiding lives in society. We have to do what we can within a reasonable means to try to provide rehabilitation because these people are going to come out of prison and they are going to be back into society.
The question is: How many of these people are going to reoffend? We do not know. In fact we do not even know how many have reoffended in the past. The Solicitor General's office used to give us that information but these statistics are mysteriously hard to come by at the present time. That is not helpful either. If we do

May 7, 1993
Government Orders
not know what we are up against, if we do not know the record of the past, then we do not know what we have to shoot for. We do not know what our objectives should be.
We are at a serious disadvantage even before we start mainly because the government is not even defining the program and is not even defining the game in which we must play and the activities in which we must participate.
One thing I think is significant in the bill is that for the first time special mention is made of the needs of aboriginal offenders, especially in relation to the use of alternate measures. We can safely say to a large degree that our correctional system has failed, more so than non-aboriginals, the aboriginal people. 'Ibis bill will not improve the situation. We are incarcerating aboriginal people much more frequently than we are incarcerating non-aboriginal people. With respect to young offenders, our aboriginal young offenders are being transferred to adult courts much more frequently than non-aboriginal offenders. With respect to women incarcerated in our correctional system, among the aboriginal women the suicide rate is incredibly high. It is a human tragedy and we have to deal with it. There has to be a better way.
There has to be a means of stopping this suicide rate which is unacceptably high among the aboriginal women in our incarceration system. We are not looking at making this system better.
We are glad this bill would oblige the consideration of a victim impact statement. Presently this is at the discretion of the courts but there seems to be a reluctance today in our correctional system to keep records and to follow these practices through, to give an accountability. We have seen it with the Parole Board and we have seen it with Correctional Services. We have seen it in our prison systems. We have seen it by the lack of information on recidivism. We just do not have information. The government does not want the public to have information. This is totally unacceptable, totally incorrect and totally counterproductive.
This bill would guarantee the prosecutor and the offender an opportunity to make submissions with respect to any fact that is relevant to sentencing. Either party could submit evidence. The court would require the production of evidence and could compel witnesses to attend and give testimony. I think that is significant. A
sentencing court under this bill would be obliged to ask whether an offender has anything to say before sentence is passed. The court would have a new obligation to record both the terms of the sentence and the reason for imposing it.
Bill C-90 does not change the existing law with respect to absolute and conditional discharges. Rules governing probation orders and intermittent custodial sentences would only be slightly changed. Existing law regarding the imposition of fines would be unchanged and courts would still imprison people for defaulting on fines.
The current domain relating to restitution remains with a few changes. One would require a sentencing court to first consider making an order of restitution rather than ordering a fine or forfeiture, especially where the offender would not have the means or ability to comply with both. Current provisions relating to imprisonment are virtually unchanged as are those governing royal prerogative of mercy and the ability of the Governor in Council to grant a conditional or free pardon.
Most of this bill has already been proposed by earlier studies and commissions. There is very little which is new. Much of it codifies the existing common law. Why was the government concerned about bringing this before the House of Commons? Why the concern? The common law has told us what needs to be done. This bill is merely codifying it. There have been numerous studies into dealing with recommendations that are brought forward at least in part by this bill. Many of the recommendations and many of the things that need to be done are not in this bill. Why is the government afraid to deal with this bill and these questions? If it is objectionable let us talk about it and let us get it before a legislative committee. The minister fails to address the concept of restructuring sentencing despite strong recommendations to do so. This bill is deficient in addition to being late.
If the government did not want that, it should have said so. Do not keep it on the back burner without any heat under it for 11 months. Withdraw it. Do not just showcase it because we are getting close to an election. It should at least show some sincerity and some leadership
May 7, 1993

with respect to its own proposed legislation in the field of sentencing.
I have some points which I think are significant and I would like to make with respect to the outline of the bill.
This proposed legislation replaces the entire section XXIII of the Criminal Code. However, in spite of it replacing the whole section it does not do a lot in improving our system of sentencing in Canada. One would think that after bringing this bill forward and after changing a whole part of the Criminal Code and after waiting 11 months that we could at least look forward to meaningful changes in sentencing in Canada. But no, it does not make major changes or improvements at all. It only touches on some of the things that need to be changed.
When the preceding Minister of Justice introduced this bill almost a year ago she promised a second stage very soon. She said that this was merely the first part of the legislation on sentencing. We have been waiting. I do not know if the government has been waiting or not, but 11 months later we just have what was introduced last June. We do not have that second part. It would make sense that if there is a second part forthcoming from the government that we would be dealing with it at the same time. It would certainly make a lot of sense to do so. We could see the whole picture.
Now we are dealing with the reluctance of the government in one part of the legislation which it does not seem to have its heart in. The stage we are dealing with now is incomplete without the second stage. The second stage, the former minister promised, assured us that it would deal with one of the biggest problems with our sentencing and correctional systems today. It is the fact that fully one-third of all prisoners in provincial and territorial jails are there for the non-payment of fines.
One-third of the total number of people in our correctional systems are there for the non-payment of fines. Among the aboriginal people it is larger than one-third.
Why are we incurring monumental costs to incarcerate people who have not paid fines? Who is paying for what? They have not paid their fines and we are paying them thousands of dollars in room and board because they have not paid their fines. It just does not make any sense.
Government Orders
Do we want to keep them shut away from society? Prison is certainly not acting as a deterrent because people still do not pay their fines. It is ludicrous. This is what the second part of this legislation was supposed to involve, the non-payment of fines. We do not have it even after waiting 11 months.
We have succeeded in creating one of the most expensive debtor prison systems in the world and the minister deferred dealing with this problem until a later date.
How complicated can this be? We are not supposed to have debtors' prisons any more yet one-third of all the people incarcerated are there because they did not pay fines and we the taxpayer are picking up the cost of this. As I said, Canada has one of the most expensive-if not the most expensive-debtor prison systems in the world.
It is now obvious that we will not have the second stage of this legislation dealing with sentencing before this Parliament is dissolved. We in the Liberal Party have promised unequivocally to rectify this situation in our recently released paper on crime and justice issues. It is really a disgrace that this question of the number of people incarcerated for the non-payment of fines has not been addressed.
Minor property or alcohol-related driving offences have accounted for the highest percentage of admissions to provincial institutions in the past several years. The offences of theft, possession of stolen goods and break and enter are the next highest offences of admission. When we talk about the fact that one-third of all the people in our correctional system are there because they did not pay a fine, followed by theft, possession of stolen goods and break and enter, then we have a large percentage of those in incarceration for which we really should be looking for alternative measures.
I want to give an idea about the cost. These people are committing crimes and they are costing a lot of money. It costs approximately $30,000 a year to keep someone in a minimum security prison. It costs $47,000 a year to keep someone in medium security. It costs $69,000 a year to keep someone in a maximum security prison. Incarceration costs for an inmate at Kingston's prison for women run over $80,000 a year. The need for change is obvious

May 7, 1993
Government Orders
especially when dealing with petty crimes such as the non-payment of fines, shoplifting and vandalism.
I am not saying that these are not important matters with which we should deal but there has to be an alternative measure in dealing with these crimes. We cannot just keep locking these people up. We just do not have the place to put them. Our correctional system cannot meet the demand. There has to be some community service. There has to be some diversion program that will have more of an impact on some of these people who think that it is funny if they commit a crime and can then just literally freeload on the Canadian taxpayers.
The correctional system was not set up to provide room and board for somebody who does not like where they are staying at the present time. We want meaningful incarceration and we want rehabilitation. We want results so these people do not commit other crimes. We want these people who commit the lesser crimes to get out and do something constructive. We want them to feel that they have to do something and be held accountable. They should meet the victims. They should be doing community service. My heavens, we need changes.
This legislation is the result of a series of special studies, reviews and commissions on sentencing dating back to 1979.
These projects were in addition to excellent work done by the now defunct Law Reform Commission on this subject. The fact that this legislation took so long in coming about is absolutely incredible. It is incredible that it has been allowed to languish on the Order Paper for 11 months. This absolutely defies all logic.
During hearings into Bill C-36, the government's weak attempt at improving our system of parole and conditional release, witness after witness said the same thing: Why has the government brought forward legislation on parole before reforming our system of sentencing?
It was obvious that sentencing should have come before parole and conditional release. The question was never answered and the result has been a piecemeal
approach to corrections and sentencing reform in Canada.
We are glad to see, however, that the minister finally recognizes that prisons should only be used as a last resort in dealing with offenders. While most people believe it will always be necessary to have prisons in our society, our over-reliance on them has become serious.
We have the second highest per capita rate of incarceration in the western world. Only the United States incarcerates more people than we do and its astounding crime rate is a testament to the fact that prisons are no answer to dealing with the crime problem.
It is interesting to look back at Canada's first Penitentiary Act. I think it is important to look at this. It was passed in 1834 and established the rationale for our first penitentiary: "If many offenders convicted of crimes were ordered to solitary imprisonment accompanied by well-regulated labour and religious instruction, it might be the means under providence, not only of deterring others from the commission of like crimes but also of reforming the individuals and inuring them with the habits of industry".
The regulations of this act establish that inmates were not to stop work or suffer their attention to be tom from it. They were not to gaze at visitors when passing through the prison nor sing, dance, whistle, jump, run or do anything which may have the slightest tendency to disturb the harmony or to contravene the rules and regulations of prisons.
This concept of correcting the inmate is still with us today, largely unchanged. Far from correcting the inmate, prison often changes the inmate for the worse, I might add, for the rest of his or her life.
We should also examine the rationale for using prisons as a means of deterrence. This is a complicated factor and should be examined in two parts: general and specific deterrence. The success of specific deterrence is seen in the recidivism rate of a particular crime.
There is even some evidence that suggests that a reverse ratio exists in some cases whereby imprisonment actually increases the likelihood of a repetition of crime. This was stated in a Law Reform Commission study in 1976.
May 7, 1993

Prison is often referred to as the post-graduate school of crime where offenders pick up pointers from other inmates, learn additional tricks of the trade and are exposed to a vety harmful inmate culture. This makes returning to the community very difficult.
While deterrents may work in some types of offences they may not work in all. One would be hard pressed today to find an expert who works in corrections who would not say that more and better rehabilitation is needed for prisoners.
While rehabilitation is one of the guiding principles of sentencing, the government fails to address its urgency and necessity. Expanding alternate measure programs such as community service, victim reconciliation and restitution to adult offenders who commit non-serious, non-violent crimes is another step which is long overdue. Actually over 20 per cent of all criminal justice expenditures in Canada go into imprisonment. Less than 1 per cent goes into community based sanctions. We in the Liberal Party believe this must change. There are neither the results nor the economic reason to keep it as it exists.
Since establishing the alternate measures program will be the responsibility of the provinces, we want assurances from the government that it will not simply offload this onto the provinces with no financial contribution. Without adequate funding these programs will never work.
There are serious problems with our system of sentencing. In closing I want to mention some of them. Sentencing judges often complain that they do not have enough non-incarceration programs on which to draw. It is therefore no surprise that our incarceration rate is so high.
Second, Canadians do not feel the criminal justice system punishes criminals severely enough, and yet conversely they overestimate the rate of violent crime in our society. Also victims feel alienated and the various agencies are said not to share information freely.
There are inconsistencies in sentencing which vary depending upon the individual judge, court or region. Resources to deal with the many offenders who require psychological treatment are scarce.
Government Orders
Why has the government waited so long before bringing this legislation forward? Why does it not include alternative measures for offenders who are jailed for non-payment of fines? Why does the minister not finally address the importance and necessity of rehabilitation programs in prison?
Lea and Young in their book What is to be done about the law and order crisis in the eighties make an observation-and I want to finish my presentation today with it-about the success of penitentiaries in achieving the objectives of making society safer and rehabilitating prisoners. They wrote: "Any hospital which made the people more sick than they originally were and where each visit made the next one more likely would have been shut down years ago".
The success of any sentencing reform will ultimately be judged by how significantly the numbers of prisoners are reduced. If there is not a substantial drop then the reforms have failed and society will have not received any benefit.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in today's debate and once again listen to the words of my hon. friend who has just spoken. I appreciated his intervention.
In looking at the Order Paper I noticed Bill C-90, the bill before us, was first introduced on June 23, 1992. Here we are almost a year later getting around to debating this legislation.
This legislation is long overdue. Canadians were clamouring for the legislation to be introduced many years ago, let alone a year ago. Here we are, essentially on the eve of an election, and the government brings forward a bill that in my judgment gives the illusion the government is getting tough on crime. It wants to improve sentencing within our Criminal Code.
I wonder how serious the government is. I noticed that the person introducing this debate at second reading today, which of course is a critical stage, was not the minister responsible. As a matter of fact it was not even the parliamentary secretary responsible. The first speaker for the government was the parliamentary secretary for international trade who read a nicely prepared statement written by somebody somewhere. It did not give the impression to anyone that the government was terribly serious about it.

May 7, 1993
Government Orders
I noticed yesterday when we were debating psychoactive substances, Bill C-85, that it was introduced by the Minister of Communications and not by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
If this legislation is important, if the government and the minister are serious about it, then why is the minister not here talking about it? Why is the minister not here to answer questions that may be put to him, questions that have already been raised in this short debate today? I guess we can set that aside and say that we are at least pleased it is now before us and we will now have a chance to debate it.
I want to preface my comments today with a quote from Sergeant Don Evers of the Saskatchewan Crime Prevention Network. He used a very striking metaphor to describe the situation confronting us today. He said: "Just as cancer eats away at people, crime eats away at our communities and societies. If we do nothing about it, it will continue to grow and it will erode everything".
There is a growing sense in the country generally that crime is increasing, that Canada is becoming a more violent society, a more violent place in which to live. I noticed a recent Maclean 'j-CTV poll which said that 50 per cent of Canadians reported their feeling of personal safety from crime had become much worse or somewhat worse over the last five years.
Fear is controlling. It restricts autonomy and can result in withdrawal from normal movement and activities. We see this when we look at particularly elderly people in our community and particularly women who are very hesitant to walk alone in their neighbourhoods after dark. Quite frankly they do not feel safe in many of our cities these days. The situation appears to be getting worse.
Back in 1989 the view that walking alone in the community after dark was unsafe was held by 33 per cent of Canadians. Today 55 per cent of women have that same attitude. There are very high levels of concern in terms of the safety of women and the elderly living particularly in the urban areas. That is the context in which we began today's debate.
When we start talking about the costs of crime, which my hon. friend has just mentioned, I have to relate a personal incident. A constituent came to see me just the other day who was absolutely and totally frustrated. He came home after work one night to find that some
people had broken into his home and had stolen some goods: VCRs, television sets and stereo sets, the usual kinds of things taken in a quick hit and run by break and enter artists.
He was frustrated and called the police. They came, wrote the usual report and said they would try to find the goods, the individuals and so on. He went out and purchased new goods: new VCRs, new television sets, et cetera. He came home the next day after work and they were all stolen. Some people had come in and stolen the same types of items from the household. He phoned the police. They came, wrote the usual report and so on. They said that they would do their best to try to find the culprits, et cetera.
He was a little hesitant to go out and buy new goods, as we can well understand. However, a few days later because he wanted a television set, a VCR and so on, he went out and replaced all the stolen goods for the second time in one week. He came back after work the next day and they were all gone again.
In other words within a handful of days he had three break and enter, and the same goods were taken. He said he was going to sit in his house with a shotgun and wait for somebody to come in. I would not condone that and nobody here would, but we can appreciate the frustration. In his view, security for him, his family and property had totally broken down.
We would all feel the same way.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
As my friend here from Regina says, we would all feel the same way. Of course we would. The police were frustrated and helpless as they cannot not sit on a doorstep and wait for someone to break into someone's house.
What they said is that often when they actually apprehend these people nothing happens to them. Part of that is a reflection of our existing laws where very young break and enter artists are not prosecuted. Also if one hires a good lawyer, the lawyer can make a case on one's behalf and often get one off scot-free. Perhaps some technicality allows one to get off or the sentencing is just a slap on the wrist. The jails are so filled up anyway that if it is a short sentence they will say just forget about it because it is not worth the hassle. So although one has actually been sentenced one does not spend any time in jail because the jails are overflowing.
May 7, 1993

I think it is fair to say that we may have a legal system where we have laws but we do not have much of a justice system. The growing perception in Canada is that we must revisit our justice system and ensure that it is doing what we intend it to do, that it accomplishes what we want it to accomplish.
I take my information from this incredibly good publication. The Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General in February of this year published Crime Prevention in Canada: Towards a National Strategy. It is its 12th report in this session of Parliament. It is excellent. If anyone is interested in this issue I would encourage them to seek out a copy.
The chair of the committee is sitting across the way and I am obviously indirectly applauding him and his colleagues from all political parties who came to a unanimous report that not only lays out the problem clearly articulated in this presentation but also a set of recommendations, from which we are already seeing legislation flowing. I stand to applaud this.
One of the useful things the committee does is identify the costs of crime. It costs taxpayers $7.7 billion to maintain the criminal justice system. An awful lot of taxpayers' money goes into maintaining this justice system. We can say it is only dollars and cents, but I think we all appreciate that crime imposes physical, emotional and psychological damage on victims either directly or indirectly that certainly cannot be quantified in monetary terms.
I am talking about people who in many cases suffer their entire lives because some trauma has occurred to them in their life, often at a very young age. On a personal basis, of course, we all know of examples where that has occurred, the tremendous cost in human agony and suffering, to say nothing of the dollars and cents loss as a result of absenteeism or illness that often leads to alcohol and drug abuse.
Also we see crime imposing a financial burden in another way, through our insurance system. Hundreds of millions of dollars, in fact billions of dollars, annually are paid out as a result of commercial or automobile thefts, again essentially being borne by the policyholders.
I think it is fair to say that we have a very serious problem in our country. We need to revisit the Young
Government Orders
Offenders Act to ensure that we see more justice attached to the young offender. I cannot help but reiterate a point made by the previous speaker.
Bring in the parents too.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
As my friend says, in many cases the parents can play more of a role.
We acknowledge that our jails are packed compared to most countries in the western world. But when one looks at the statistics in terms of the rate for 100,000 the United States tops the list. There are 426 people per 100,000 in a jail of some kind. We are next in line. We drop a long way down to 112 people per 100,000 in jail. In the United Kingdom it is 97 per 100,000; in France it is 80; Australia it is 78; Sweden it is 56; in the Netherlands it is 40 and so on down the line.
Often in our public gatherings and meetings-my friend from Regina will certainly confirm this-people suggest that we need more jails. We need to put more people in jail to reduce the level of crime. If that were the case, I think we would all acknowledge then that the safest place to live on earth would be the United States.
This is rather revealing. In 1991 the United States Senate judiciary committee described the United States as the most violent and self-destructive nation on earth. Their own elected representatives describe their country as the most violent and self-destructive nation on earth. The committee concluded from FBI data on violence that in 1990 the United States led the entire world with in murders, rapes and robberies. Every hour approximately 200 Americans become victims of violence.
It is called free enterprise.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
In other words, simply placing people in jail is not the way to have a more secure society. It is not the way to reduce crime. Otherwise the United States would be a very friendly, happy, crime-free place, which of course is the exact opposite of the truth.
One-third of the people who are in jails today are not there because they have carried out some violent crime or even major crime. Often they are there because they have been caught on some petty offence and are simply unable to pay the fine. A lot of Canadians, if their fine is

May 7, 1993
Government Orders
$1,000, $2,000 or $3,000, are simply unable to come up with that kind of cash and so they head into jails.
What does it cost? Not only are they not paying then-fines, but it costs about $30,000 a year to maintain them in a minimum security institution. If they are going into medium security, it costs about $47,000 and if they are going into maximum security it is $69,000 annually. Obviously this is a rather absurd way to spend taxpayers' money. To punish someone who has not paid a fine costs taxpayers many tens of thousands of dollars on an annual basis.
We need alternatives to those institutions, alternative places for judges to sentence people who have committed some crime, often of a petty nature-I will not go into all the petty crimes-yet are unable to pay the fines.
Those who are in jail in the United States overwhelmingly tend to be black people. In Canada overwhelmingly they tend to be aboriginal people. Often they do not have access to high priced lawyers or cannot come up with the cash for their fines or for a whole set of obvious reasons, sociological reasons, cultural reasons. Yet we somehow feel that the appropriate thing to do is to sentence aboriginal people to a jail sentence which, as my friend has indicated, often is considered to be the post-graduate school for the criminal.
There is not much choice.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
For them of course, as my friend from Regina once again says, there is no choice.
In that context I will say a few words about Bill C-90 directly, an act to amend the Criminal Code (sentencing). I want to apologize on behalf of my colleague from Port Moody-Coquitlam who has spent a lot of time in this area and knows it like the back of his hand. He wanted to be here today to participate in the debate, but since it was kind of sprung on us, he was unable to because of other commitments. That is the reality. Therefore I am here to say a few words on his behalf. I will not be able to do the job half as well as he could have.
Bill C-90 has been widely anticipated as the companion legislation to the Corrections and Conditional Release Act which we call Bill C-36 which received royal assent back in June 1992. It represents the federal government's belated response to two landmark reports. One was by the Canadian Sentencing Commission which
you will remember, Mr. Speaker, from 1987 and the other by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General was called Taking Responsibility back in 1988. It was an excellent report, I might add.
If passed, the bill would constitute the first major statutory set of revisions to sentencing in over 125 years. That is really quite a comment in terms of where we stand today. We are obviously totally out of whack with the real world. Our sentencing provisions do not make any sense. Judges complain because they have no alternative areas to send people through sentencing. It just goes on and on. It is a total disaster.
We have waited years for this to happen but at least it is happening today. My recollection is that the most recent attempt was Bill C-19 which died on the Order Paper way back in 1984.
This bill includes a statement of the purpose and principles of sentencing, provisions dealing with the imposition of alternative measures, amendments to the procedural aspects of sentencing, the sections addressing judicial control over parole eligibility dates, and so on and so forth. I do not have to go into detail. Mr. Speaker, you and others are well aware of the specifics.
There are parts of this bill that I want to refer to specifically because they have been received very positively. I am trying to find some good news in today's afternoon agenda. Section 717 advocates the increased use of alternative dispositions for adult offenders. That is an excellent step in the right direction, and one that we are all pleased to finally see.
Another aspect of the bill is Section 726.2 which represents a clear call for judges to state the reasons for the sentences they choose on a given case and to have these entered into the record of proceedings. Such a requirement would help to make a contribution to increasing the understanding of those concerned with the sentencing process including those involved themselves, the appeal courts, the media and the public generally.
If there is one thing that is puzzling about our judicial, legal world today it is the whole matter of sentencing. One person will commit a heinous crime in society's judgement and get off with a little slap on the wrist while somebody else who might be caught with a little sample
May 7, 1993

of marijuana in their truck will end up in jail for 10 years. It is absolutely incredible. We must bring some rhyme or reason to the sentencing system. If there is one thing that we all agree upon, I do not think there is a single Canadian who has looked at this aspect at all who would not say that this call for judges to state the reasons for their sentences and to have these entered into the record of proceedings is an absolutely critical step to take.
Another provision, section 719, provides that terms of imprisonment are to begin on the day on which the convicted person was taken into custody. Again this is a very positive initiative. How many times are people taken into custody and spend a lot of time in custody and then are given their sentence after they have been there for perhaps many, many months? It is unfortunate and is something we condemn in other jurisdictions and something that we really need to revisit here. We are pleased to see that in the bill.
The former Minister of Justice, the present Minister of National Defence who is running for the Conservative leadership, also promised that she would bring forward part two, or what she has called the second phase of this legislation, dealing specifically with fines and intermediate sanctions.
The use of alternative disposition for adult offenders makes a lot of sense when one examines the existing situation. Provincial jails in this country have too often become debtors' prisons. As I said earlier, almost one-third of the people are there because they have defaulted on fines. Certainly failing to pay a fine is a serious concern and the law is not to be flouted, but failing to pay a fine is no indication that the offender is too dangerous to live in the community. A prison sentence for failing to pay a fine is an unjustifiable cost to the taxpayer. The community feels no greater security and the offender is no more capable of paying the fine upon release. Therein lies the need to have some alternative to simply placing somebody behind bars because they failed to pay a fine.
The costs vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. However taking a modest approximation of $75 per day per inmate, someone sentenced to a $300 fine or 14-day sentence who ends up in prison costs the state a maximum of $1,050. Any legislation that will allow the
Government Orders
courts to seek alternatives such as community service work would be a welcome initiative indeed.
The former minister promised a speedy introduction of phase two when the bill we are now debating was introduced almost a year ago. It has taken close to one year for this bill to progress from first to second reading, not a record setting pace by any means. I would certainly urge the current Minister of Justice to consider breaking a few records and bring forward phase two of this initiative in this session of Parliament so we can at least begin the process and hopefully even complete it.
While certain aspects of the bill before us have been recognized and lauded as thoughtful and progressive, significant concern has been expressed about what is missing from this initiative. In a Bill C-90 press release the Department of Justice promises that:
These reforms, along with correctional reform Bill C-36 which
became law last week, are aimed at providing a co-ordinated and
comprehensive overhaul of the Canadian criminal justice system.
In reality there is every likelihood that this legislation will have no or very little real impact on day to day sentencing in the courts.
Julian Roberts, who is presently with the University of Ottawa and worked as a research analyst on the Canadian sentencing reform commission and appeared as a witness before the standing committee's hearings in 1988, states in an as of yet to be published review of the bill that:
Bill C-90 represents not so much real, but rather illusory change.
In other words, the indication is that this is not a serious and real initiative.
I see that my time is up. Again I want to say that there is so much more to say to point out the weaknesses of this legislation. I apologize that my colleague, the NDP justice critic, the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, was unable to be here. However during the committee stage of this legislation he will point out ways and means in which he feels it should be improved so that it can be brought up to the year 1993 and prepared for sentencing beyond the year 2000.

Mr. Speaker, it is important when we debate this bill and look

Government Orders
at it to understand and question why the government waited a year before it brought this bill back.
Is it that we are close to an election? Is it that the government of the day wants to side-track us from what is really out there?
Four years ago the minister said that we were going to revamp the Young Offenders Act. I quote word for word from the throne speech:
The need to protect the society is far more important than the need
to protect the young offender.
That need has been there for the past four years, yet the government has been busy with NAFTA. It has been busy with this and the government has been busy with that. All of a sudden, it is the eve of an election and the government comes out with this second reading of Bill C-90.
The hon. member for Scarborough Centre sends out a householder that deals with nothing else but penalties and the legal system while she again side-tracks from the real issue.
Four years ago I introduced private member's Bill C-26, which would have made amendments to the Young Offenders Act. At that time the members of the government and of the NDP said: Forget it. It is not a real thing. It should not fly. It should not do this and it should not do that. It was killed on second reading.
Yet that bill had good initiatives which the government of the day stole and tried to implement but the implementation was not there. I want to revisit why that bill was introduced.
A young offender in my riding of Scarborough-Agin-court committed a triple murder and received a maximum of three years. The people of this land, the people of my riding rose to their feet and there was a public outcry and changes were necessary. Changes were brought forward. They included: first, murder over the age 14 meant automatic transfer to the adult court; second, mandatory treatment; and third, for other crimes besides murder five years less a day for all penalties.
My question to the member of the third party is the following. Does he not agree with me that the government of the day is playing politics with us by waiting exactly one year before it brought this bill back again because it wants to side-track us from what is really out
there? It wants to side-track us from the real issue of dealing with the economy. It should have dealt with this a long time ago.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has hit the nail on the head.
I think it is fair to say that considering this legislation was introduced 11 months ago after years and years of the public calling for changes to the Criminal Code regarding sentencing and we are now in the dying moments of this political mandate to this government and there is a lot of work to be done.
